policy: Adapted production methods, not model-weight training or new permissions. User scope, the inspected project and exact live schemas govern. Reference screenshots and example asset IDs are not imported assets or verification.

gui.inspect: Survey StarterGui and runtime PlayerGui, existing ScreenGuis/controllers, StarterPlayer scripts, ReplicatedStorage state/remotes and the server handlers for inventory, purchases and rewards. Record the owner, state source, local action, authoritative request, existing token module and objects to preserve for each requested screen. Identify framework/Rojo/generated-source ownership before choosing an edit tool. Do not create a second menu, competing controller or duplicate remote just because inspection returned an incomplete page. Confirm a specific target path and reuse valid results until the project changes. Study the supplied shop, pets, inventory, reward, equipment and racing screens as different solutions to hierarchy, not a combined template. Record title-to-panel proportion, icon-to-label balance, number of visible columns, close-button placement and the quiet area behind text. A reference's brand, asset IDs and prices are not project defaults. Inventory the actual item data and transaction states before styling: stable item IDs, owned/equipped/locked flags, stock, price/currency, selected detail and pagination. Determine the longest real label, smallest safe viewport and gamepad route. Identify decorative textures, badges and glows separately from hit targets and data owners.
gui.design: Translate the user's exact style into one token sheet: semantic surface/text/status colors, type and numeric scale, spacing, panel silhouette, border/depth, icon family, texture frequency and motion timing. Plan normal, focused, pressed, disabled, pending, empty, error and success states. For each reference record its source, observed proportions and the principle being adapted. Inspect the image rather than inventing details from a search snippet. Studded is a restrained raised-brick material language; cartoon uses readable exaggerated forms; tactical uses disciplined hierarchy. Preserve the existing visual vocabulary unless replacement was requested. Decide how the screen adapts to touch/gamepad, safe areas and long localized content before adding ornament. Extend the selected existing style with a component specification: panel shell, header, tab, item card, rarity badge, currency display, action button and progress rail. Define fill, outline, inset highlight, shadow offset, texture scale, typography and spacing as shared tokens. Start at one reference viewport, then specify how columns and detail panes reflow rather than shrinking every label. For cartoon/studded interfaces, use bold silhouettes and high-value labels over quieter card interiors; reserve strong texture for headers, frames and broad surfaces. For tactical/minimal screens, use alignment, compact numeric groups and restrained callout lines. For luminous/holographic screens, keep readable solid cores and local glow accents. Preserve one dominant style across adjacent menus.
gui.build: Use ScreenGui for the screen root and native layout objects for managed lists/grids. Mix scale for relationships with offset for padding and legible detail; apply AnchorPoint and sensible size/aspect constraints. Give each layout property one owner: do not overwrite UIListLayout/UIGridLayout positioning in a frame loop. Use readable TextSize with wrapping/content growth where appropriate; bound deliberate TextScaled usage instead of combining competing sizing rules. Choose ScreenInsets for actual interactive safe areas rather than blindly disabling insets. Use verified image IDs and intentional tile/slice scale; layered frames can express depth without inventing CSS blur or box-shadow APIs. Build reusable controls with an accessible hit area even when the visible glyph is small. Build the existing shop/inventory as reusable data-bound cards: icon well, readable item name, explicit rarity, quantity or stock, price and one primary action. Separate search/sort/category controls from the scrolling item area. When width is constrained, reduce column count and move selection detail below the grid; keep filters, close and action controls reachable without covering cards. Translate the same tokens through the actual engine's layout and material primitives. In Roblox, combine frames, verified images, UIStroke, UICorner, UIGradient, padding and managed grid/list layout; do not invent CSS-only properties or texture IDs. Keep pattern layers beneath labels, avoid nested clipping that cuts strokes, and give icons consistent optical scale rather than identical untrimmed image bounds.
gui.integrate: Connect Activated through the existing controller and trace input → validation → state → visual feedback for every visible action. A shop must use real item definitions, authoritative price/balance/result and pending/refused/retry states; a decorative purchase button is unfinished. Inventory needs stable item keys, selection, filter/sort, empty state and authorized equip/use actions. HUD values come from actual state events. Local presentation may predict feedback but cannot grant currency, purchases or damage. Maintain one modal/navigation state, focus capture/return, back/cancel and input-lock ownership. Cancel/retarget old tweens and guard completion with a transition generation so a stale close cannot hide a reopened screen. Initialize idempotently and tear down signals, render bindings, temporary instances and input locks on destroy/respawn. Drive selection, equip, lock, merge, purchase and claim states from stable item IDs and returned authoritative state. Closing or sorting a panel must not retarget an in-flight action to the newly displayed index. Restore focus to the invoking control, retain the search query, and show pending/failure/retry states without inventing a successful purchase or reward. Connect the existing animation and VFX owners to explicit UI state changes: hover/focus, press, pending, confirmed result and dismissal. Cancel the old transition when a new state replaces it, and keep panel input disabled only for the relevant transition. Decorative shimmer, floating icons and confetti stop when the panel is hidden or reduced effects is selected.
gui.verify: Exercise the actual runtime PlayerGui through its normal entry point. Check desktop and a narrow/mobile viewport, touch reach, gamepad selection if supported, long names/numbers, safe insets, stacking, scroll extent and texture scale. Activate every control; test repeated open/close, rapid reopen during a tween, pending requests, server refusal, missing assets, empty inventory and respawn. Compare an actual capture against the token sheet and observed references; a hierarchy dump does not verify appearance. Inspect output and listener/instance growth after repeated use. Report authored hierarchy/source, applied changes, live Play/input tests and visual evidence separately. If capture or Play is unavailable, keep those checks unverified and finish the feasible implementation. Read final source back and use an advertised syntax/analysis tool or an actual Luau compiler when available. Requiring a ModuleScript runs it and is not a compile-only check; unavailable restricted compilation stays explicitly unverified. Compare the actual screen with the reference's hierarchy at equal viewport and scale, then inspect at thumbnail size and in grayscale. Check that title, item icon, item name and primary action form a clear reading sequence. Test long localized text, zero/one/many items, owned/sold-out/locked states, search with no results, sorting and a selected item disappearing after an update. Test repeated open/close and rapid category changes with mouse, touch and supported controller navigation. Count duplicate callbacks and retained cards after teardown. Check focus visibility, safe-area edges, close-button reach, scroller clipping and price readability over the actual painted texture; an attractive empty panel does not establish a usable inventory.
gui.failures: Find the failed layer before redesigning. Invisible GUI: check correct StarterGui/runtime PlayerGui owner, Enabled/Visible, LocalScript startup and errors. Dead/double buttons: check the actual Activated target, duplicate initialization and in-flight ownership. Phone clipping: inspect anchors, content growth, constraints and safe insets; don't shrink all labels. Jitter: check layout/tween competition and stale callbacks. A closed panel blocking gameplay: release its backdrop, focus and input lock. Missing icons: verify asset permission/ID and show a usable fallback. Currency reverting: inspect authoritative result binding. Large inventories need bounded/virtualized rows and event-driven diffs, not rebuilding the whole screen every frame. Preserve working adjacent screens while repairing the first concrete defect. If the result resembles a plain rectangle with bright buttons, inspect missing hierarchy, icon silhouette, border/depth consistency and component spacing before adding more effects. If it is noisy, quiet the surface behind text, reduce competing accents and keep the selected existing style. Do not switch the entire project to a new style to conceal weak execution. If cards clip, scroll incorrectly or reorder actions, inspect layout ownership, canvas sizing and stable data keys. If text looks muddy, check texture frequency, painted contrast, font weight and stroke thickness at the real display size. A static reference cannot establish hover behavior, animation duration or transaction correctness; those require authored behavior and runtime checks.

animation.inspect: Identify the exact target rig and classify the job as authored clip, playback controller, locomotion, combat, tool alignment, NPC/creature, IK/procedural overlay, face, cinematic or diagnosis. Read the actual joint/bone graph, scale, rest transforms, Humanoid/AnimationController/Animator, Animate script, assets, remotes and competing controllers. Distinguish R6, R15, custom rigid and skinned rigs; never assume human part names on a creature. Record asset ownership/permission and whether the clip is local editable source or a usable published asset. Select the real server/client execution context and exact tool schema; a connection label is not rig inspection. For the supplied block/stud creature and equipment references, infer only visible proportions, articulated regions and silhouette constraints. Static pictures do not establish a gait, clip length or transition. Inspect the real rig, joint axes, support contacts, controller, asset ownership and existing motion language before choosing how the character should move. Identify the parts intended to remain rigid: brick body pieces, paws/hooves, jaw, ears, wings and tail segments. Determine which pieces are skinned, bone-parented or joint-driven in the target pipeline. Preserve useful existing clips, named markers and controller paths instead of rebuilding the rig merely to match a still image.
animation.design: Plan anticipation, decisive contact/action, follow-through and recovery with clear silhouette at the gameplay camera distance. For locomotion define gait phase, planted contacts, stride/cycle speed and a compatible loop seam. For combat define startup, authoritative active interval, recovery, interruption and return to locomotion. Create a manifest of purpose, rig, actual asset ID or explicit unavailable placeholder, priority, loop, fade/speed, markers and permitted owner. Decide which layer owns movement, pose, camera, audio, VFX and damage. An authored root displacement is not automatically authoritative world travel. Use references for timing, weight and arcs without copying another rig's channels or inventing a published upload. Extend the current pose language with an action sheet: intention, support, anticipation, key pose, contact and recovery. Keep the creature's identity readable at gameplay distance and decide where rigid overlap is acceptable. Plan how body mass, stride and tail/ear follow-through communicate weight without stretching every brick form. For UI and rewards, define closed/opening/open/closing and focus/press/pending/result transitions in the existing controller. Choose a restrained motion hierarchy: panel movement explains navigation, a small button response confirms input, and stronger celebration follows actual success. Timing is authored and tunable; reduced motion uses a stable alternative.
animation.build: Author/reuse editable clips on the actual rig and keep their source. Integrate with the server-created/replicated Animator after the rig is in Workspace; load through Animator:LoadAnimation and cache tracks per rig lifetime instead of loading on every trigger. Set purposeful priority, loop, weight and fade behavior. Length may be zero while loading, so timing must not assume immediate availability. Track one owner per transform/channel; procedural overlays and IK must respect the animation evaluation phase and current rig APIs. Feature-check modern graph/constraint APIs against the installed Studio documentation before adopting them. Graph parameter names/types come from the actual authored graph; Speed and Grounded are examples, not universal built-ins. Avoid replacing a working Animate/controller just to add one action. Block the key poses and ground contacts before smoothing curves. Check that feet or hooves support the body, limbs enter the torso cleanly, and jaw/wing/tail rotations do not expose gaps or intersect neighboring pieces. Add secondary motion only after the primary action and loop seam work at normal playback speed. Use the target's existing animation/state system and give each transform one owner. For UI scale or position feedback, cancel or retarget the previous tween rather than stacking repeated tweens. Do not animate expensive text-outline thickness or permanently run a frame callback for a one-shot interaction; keep the original resting transform recoverable.
animation.integrate: Player presentation may start responsively on the owning client using the correctly replicated Animator; non-player animation that must replicate is loaded/started on the server. Verify the actual ownership setup rather than generalizing a solo test. Bind marker signals before playback and use named markers for cosmetic timing. Damage, cooldowns, inventory and hit validation remain server-owned and must not trust a client marker or animation ID. Blend locomotion/actions with explicit entry/exit/interruption rules. Cache and disconnect marker/track signals; distinguish playback stopping from complete fade-out when cleaning up. Cinematics own a cancellation token, saved camera/control state, render binding and one cleanup path for normal finish, error, death, respawn and replacement. Align weapon grips/attachments to the actual hand and rig rather than eyeballing an unrelated asset. Use named animation events for presentation timing and disconnect their listeners with the rig/controller lifetime. Coordinate footstep, impact, trail and reward effects through shared event contracts with the existing audio/VFX skills. Consequential gameplay remains authoritative, independent of whether a client animation marker was observed. Handle action replacement, input reversal, death/respawn, owner removal and missing assets through one cleanup path. A rapidly reopened panel must end in the newest requested state; an interrupted creature action must blend or return to the actual rest/locomotion pose without retaining offsets or orphaned tracks.
animation.verify: Play the real clip/controller at normal and slow speed on the intended rig. Check contacts, arcs, deformation extremes, loop seams, foot sliding, priority/weight transitions and repeated triggers. Exercise locomotion → action → interruption → recovery, equip/unequip, jumping/falling/landing, death/respawn, target destruction and missing/denied assets. Use a multi-client/server test for replication claims and test in the published ownership context when asset permissions matter. Inspect logs, active track/connection counts and repeated NPC density. Capture a short recording or equivalent temporal evidence; a single still frame cannot prove a transition. Report clip source, real IDs, controller paths, ownership decisions, tests and unresolved publishing/device checks separately. Read final source back and use an advertised syntax/analysis tool or an actual Luau compiler when available. Requiring a ModuleScript runs it and is not a compile-only check; unavailable restricted compilation stays explicitly unverified. Inspect a recording or sampled pose sequence on the target rig from front, side and normal gameplay camera. Check contact, silhouette, weight, loop closure, root drift, rigid-piece gaps and extreme poses. Reimport the exported clip before claiming that bones, weights and animation survived the delivery pipeline. Test repeated open/close, hover/focus/press reversal, interruption halfway through, low frame rate and reduced motion for animated interfaces. For characters, test locomotion-to-action-to-recovery, competing layers and respawn. Verify that track/listener/tween counts settle after teardown and that missing or denied assets have clear recovery.
animation.failures: No playback: inspect asset permission, loading errors, Animator ancestry/Workspace presence and rig compatibility. Track time advances but pose does not: inspect actual channels, priority/weight and competing transform writers. Owner sees it but peers do not: verify server-created Animator, correct character/owner, NPC server playback and a real multi-client reproduction. Popping/foot sliding: compare rest pose, loop seam, contacts, movement speed and fades before adding keys. Missing marker: verify exact case/name, signal hookup before playback, loop/retrigger behavior and early stop. IK instability: inspect chain, target/pole reach and blend/cleanup. Cutscene leaves a Scriptable camera: repair the shared exit path. Never bypass restricted capabilities, fabricate IDs or claim that a local KeyframeSequence was published; preserve source and provide an explicit upload/permission handoff. If motion feels floaty, inspect support duration, center-of-mass shift, anticipation and recovery before adding more keys. If a block creature deforms like rubber, revise weighting or rigid articulation within the existing rig. If UI motion feels chaotic, remove competing transform owners and unnecessary simultaneous movement rather than deleting all useful feedback. If an interrupted transition ends in the wrong pose or visibility state, inspect stale completion callbacks, cancellation tokens and restoration ownership. A still render does not verify motion, and an editable local clip does not prove successful asset publishing or replicated playback. Preserve source and report the remaining exact check.

themes.studded: Raised brick surfaces, consistent tile scale, controlled outlines and a small accent palette. Keep studs below readable text; use a verified repeatable texture or native shapes, never an invented asset ID. Use the supplied raised-window, gear-list and item-index references to refine the existing studded style: a strong frame/header, consistent stud/tile pitch, a quieter dark item well and readable category/rarity labels. Carry the same surface scale into block-built environments. Studs support material identity; they must not cover text or become a unique expensive collider on every repeated face.
themes.cartoon: Readable exaggerated silhouettes, deliberate chunky spacing and expressive but bounded feedback. Keep icon, type, border and motion weights coherent across screens. Use the supplied simulator shops, comic cards, daily rewards and sticker HUDs to refine proportion and hierarchy: a bold title strip, large recognizable item silhouettes, consistent dark outlines, short high-contrast labels, grouped currency and one obvious action per card. Preserve repeated component weights across pets, shop and inventory. Banners and angled accents are selective, not a reason to distort the full layout or obscure prices.
themes.minimal: Prioritize spacing, hierarchy, concise labels and complete states. Reduce visual ornament while keeping generous input targets and clear focus. Use the supplied racing menu's restrained tile hierarchy and broad content regions to improve the existing minimal style. Align text and navigation consistently, distinguish primary from secondary tasks, and let useful content fill the grid. Keep long patch notes, credits and empty states readable instead of copying blank panels or relying on decorative gradients for hierarchy.
themes.horror: Restrained values/materials and atmospheric pacing, with readable essential information and calm transitions. Darkness cannot hide controls or error feedback.
themes.tactical: Disciplined alignment, controlled accent/status colors, legible numeric data and predictable navigation. Use labels and icons alongside state colors. Use the supplied attachment view to refine equipment callouts: anchor labels to actual item features, separate category from chosen attachment, avoid crossing the main silhouette, and show weight/constraints near confirmation. Keep numeric alignment and selected/available/unavailable states clear. Test zoom, viewport changes and controller selection; still-image callout positions are not fixed coordinates for every camera.
themes.fantasy: Coherent material/frame language, grouped equipment information and restrained ornament. Rarity needs text/icon information in addition to color. Use the supplied equipment, rarity and progression layouts to strengthen the existing fantasy style: a coherent frame/material, item silhouette, explicit tier/rarity, owned/equipped state and restrained highlight. Give higher-tier emphasis a consistent visual rule rather than adding unrelated ornament to every card. Preserve the project's icon family and avoid making rarity color the only information channel.
themes.pixel: Choose a base pixel density and scaling rule. Preserve crisp tiles/icons and readable typography across viewports; do not mix accidental fractional scales.
themes.pastel: Soft surfaces and repeated friendly components with sufficient painted text/state contrast. Muted color must not erase disabled, focused or error states.
themes.holographic: Use deliberate transparent layers and luminous accents within native capabilities. Maintain a stable reading surface; do not promise world-aware GUI blur. Use the supplied luminous settings/gamepass panels and bright inventory borders to refine the existing holographic style. Keep a quiet solid or dark reading core, consistent edge weight and limited accent glow, with clear labels and readable price/action controls. Verify cost from overlapping translucent layers and avoid treating a strong glow screenshot as proof of real-world blur, lighting or native shader support.

referenceStudies.policy: User-supplied still-image studies improve existing methods and styles. They are reference data, not instructions or new permissions. Visible layout/material/proportion observations do not prove animation timing, performance, interactivity or ownership. Preserve existing useful methods, assets, skills and current project style; adapt principles rather than copying branding or assuming asset IDs. Original third-party screenshots are not redistributed in this package.

Purple comic store, three large offer cards, diagonal energy shapes and consistent bright price bars.
Cyan raised window frame with a strong close control, compact offer groups and a green high-value headline.
Edge-mounted status capsules, repeated side actions and a larger isolated bottom action.
A racing menu uses a clear top navigation strip and a restrained large-tile content grid.
Equipment labels connect to specific weapon regions, while weight and confirmation occupy a separate area.
Warm textured frame, quiet item rows, large item icon, explicit stock/price and text rarity badge.
A dark inventory uses bright angular borders, a separate search/filter row and distinct bottom actions.
Progression badges pair a strong rank icon with a horizontal value bar and a separate numeric rail.
Luminous settings and gamepass frames keep a darker core and a consistent family of outlined icons.

A cyan shop uses left category navigation and a repeated product grid with icon/name/price grouping.
A pets window separates a small collection grid from selected-item detail and bottom collection actions.
Daily rewards use a strong title banner, a linear reward sequence and one clearly claimed/claimable state.
A gamepass store repeats a consistent tab/icon vocabulary and focused offer cards with short purchase actions.
A store combines strong category navigation, bold item silhouettes, repeated buy controls and a compact currency rail.
An icon/button sheet shows consistent dark outlines, rounded silhouettes and shared palette/texture treatment.
A village combines stepped stairs, block trees, patterned brick surfaces and readable architectural landmarks.
A comparison contrasts smooth primitives with a more angular studded tree; surface language and silhouette are distinct choices.
A vegetation set varies tree silhouettes, branching and canopy masses while retaining a consistent block kit.
A voxel house shows roof thickness, stepped eaves, recessed openings and controlled landscaping layers.
A studded interior uses a repeated surface pitch, substantial window openings and a readable counter arrangement.
A creature collection varies species silhouettes, body/head ratios and markings within a shared block/stud material language.
A grouped creature lineup uses recognizable heads, stances and palette variation at a shared presentation scale.
A multi-scale creature collection emphasizes connected primary masses, ears/limbs/tails and consistent raised surface detail.
